claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys with significant atomic-size mismatch develop persistent lattice distortions.
Persistent lattice distortions slow atomic diffusion.
Significant atomic-size mismatch promotes grain-boundary pinning.
Slower diffusion and grain-boundary pinning enhance structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
The initial nanoalloy is well mixed and has a uniform room-temperature elemental distribution.
Lattice distortions and grain-boundary pinning persist during high-temperature annealing.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain hinders atomic diffusion through a sluggish-diffusion effect.
Hindered atomic diffusion produces slower grain growth.
Hindered atomic diffusion reduces phase segregation.
Reduced grain growth and phase segregation maintain structural and chemical integrity.
After identical high-temperature annealing, the high-size-mismatch nanoalloy will exhibit slower grain growth than the lower-size-mismatch baseline.
After identical high-temperature annealing, the high-size-mismatch nanoalloy will exhibit less phase separation than the baseline.
After identical high-temperature annealing, the high-size-mismatch nanoalloy will retain a more homogeneous elemental distribution than the baseline.
The proposed comparison uses a baseline nanoalloy with similar overall composition but lower atomic-size mismatch under the same thermal conditions.
The prediction is limited primarily to nanoalloys having both high configurational entropy and significant atomic-size differences.
Lower-entropy alloys or alloys with minimal size mismatch may not display the predicted stability improvement.
Failure to observe significantly slower grain growth, reduced phase segregation, and a more uniform elemental distribution in the high-mismatch sample would falsify the proposed mechanism.
